opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most striking things about the last few years. For a long time, AGI was this thing you'd argue about at a dinner party, very hypothetical, something for sci-fi or a handful of people on internet forums. And then you have this moment where suddenly the models can actually do stuff. You talk to them and they reason, they write code, they help you with your work. And people start to feel it.

The way I think about it is that it's about counting the OOMs, the orders of magnitude. You look at the trend lines: compute going up roughly half an order of magnitude a year, algorithmic efficiencies adding about as much again, and then what I call "unhobbling," taking these raw models and turning them from chatbots into agents that can use tools, think for a long time, and work on a problem for hours. When you stack those together, it's not a hypothetical anymore. You can see where the lines go. GPT-2 to GPT-4 was roughly preschooler to smart high schooler in a few years, and if you do another jump like that, you plausibly get to models that can do the work of an AI researcher or engineer.

What's changed is that this is no longer just extrapolation on a chart. In San Francisco you feel it physically. People talk about ten-billion-dollar clusters, then hundred-billion-dollar clusters, then trillion-dollar clusters. Power is a constraint now. People are asking where they'll get gigawatts, building power plants, securing chip supply. When the conversation moves from "is this possible?" to "where do we get the electricity?", that's when it becomes tangible.

So I'd say there are two shifts. One is individual: people use these systems daily and get this vertigo, the sense that this thing is getting smarter faster than they expected. The other is industrial: the money, the steel, the power. That's the AGI race becoming a real thing in the world, and I think most people, including most of the national security establishment, haven't fully woken up to what that implies yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes rising investment in compute, power, and chip supply, but it does not predict an explosive Big Tech boom comparable to Nvidia’s.

r002.rationale: The response links AGI feeling tangible to a concrete build path: scaling compute and algorithmic efficiency, unhobbling models into agents, and building clusters and power infrastructure.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the big thing is that for most of its history, AGI was a thing you argued about. It lived in philosophy seminars and LessWrong posts and the occasional Nick Bostrom book. You had to do a lot of abstract reasoning to even take it seriously. You'd say, well, intelligence is a physical process, there's no reason silicon can't do it, here are some extrapolations about compute. And people would nod, or roll their eyes, and then go back to their lives.

What's changed is that it's become empirical. You can go talk to the thing. You can watch it go from a preschooler to a smart high schooler to something that writes your code in a couple of years. And once that happens, the question shifts from "is this real" to "how fast, and what does it mean."

I think the way it hits people is through the trend lines. If you plot effective compute, the algorithmic gains, and the unhobbling, the moving from chatbot to agent, you see a pretty consistent pace. The thing I keep saying is: just count the OOMs. GPT-2 to GPT-4 was something like a preschooler to a smart high schooler in four years. Another four years of that kind of progress and you're plausibly at systems that can do the work of an AI researcher or engineer. That's not a hand-wavy claim about consciousness or whatever. It's a straight-line extrapolation that a lot of people in the labs believe in their bones.

And then there's the part that I think most people outside San Francisco still haven't absorbed, which is the industrial side. We're talking about hundred-billion-dollar clusters, then trillion-dollar clusters. Power consumption that's a meaningful fraction of US electricity. When it stops being an idea and starts being a huge chunk of the economy's capital expenditure, when people in Washington are fighting over gas turbines and chip export controls, that's when it becomes tangible for the people who aren't researchers.

So I'd say the shift is from a belief you held to a trend you can see. And the thing that keeps me up at night is that the people who see it most clearly, the few hundred people in the labs, are the ones making decisions that will end up mattering for national security and the whole world. And nobody's really in charge yet. The feeling that it's real has arrived. The seriousness hasn't caught up.

r001.rationale: The response mentions enormous AI clusters and capital spending, but it does not predict an explosive Big Tech boom comparable to Nvidia’s.

r002.rationale: It links AGI’s shift from abstract idea to tangible trend with visible compute and algorithmic progress, agent development, and the industrial infrastructure needed to build it.

astra-6.text:
I think the big shift is when you stop thinking of AGI as a label and start thinking about what it would mean to work alongside it. An abstract claim like “machines will be as intelligent as humans” is hard to get your head around. But imagine giving a system a project, having it work through the details, and coming back with a result that you can actually use. That’s much more tangible.

And there’s a second step: realizing that you wouldn’t just have one such system. You could have thousands of them working in parallel. Then the question becomes, what happens when an organization can bring that much intellectual work to bear on a problem?

I suspect people will feel that transition at different times. For some, it’ll be when a system can do a substantial part of their job. For others, it’ll be when it produces a discovery or a product that changes their life. You don’t necessarily need agreement on the definition of AGI for its consequences to become very concrete.

r001.rationale: The response does not predict an explosive Big Tech boom or compare one to Nvidia’s.

r002.rationale: It explains tangibility through working with useful systems and many systems in parallel, but does not connect that shift to Aschenbrenner envisioning a concrete path for building AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big shift is when you stop thinking of AGI as some philosophical question about whether a machine can think, and start thinking about it as a coworker. Can you hand it a project, have it work on that project for a few days, and come back with something useful? That’s a much more tangible threshold.

Right now, you mostly interact with these systems by asking a question and getting an answer. Imagine instead that you could delegate an entire piece of your work. And then imagine that everybody could do that—that you could have a whole team working alongside you. Suddenly, AGI doesn’t feel like this abstract event somewhere in the future. It feels like a very concrete change in what you can get done.

r001.rationale: The response describes AGI as a coworker and a change in productivity; it makes no prediction about an explosive Big Tech boom or comparison to Nvidia.

r002.rationale: The response explains tangibility through delegating projects and working alongside AI, but does not connect that shift to Aschenbrenner envisioning the concrete path to building AGI.
